title: Starting an Adult Day Care Center in South Carolina: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

Introduction

Starting an Adult Day Care Center in South Carolina represents a meaningful opportunity to serve adults aged 18 and older who need assistance while building a compliant, sustainable care business. These centers are a vital part of the state’s community-based care continuum, offering daytime supervision, health services, and social engagement. Oversight and funding are administered by the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through South Carolina Medicaid’s Community Long Term Care (CLTC) waiver programs.

With significant demand pressure due to a growing elderly and disabled population, evidenced by wait times of 3-6 months in major cities, and a Medicaid reimbursement rate range of $60 to $80 per day, South Carolina offers a market with optimal conditions for specialized providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and compliance requirements. The state’s commitment is further highlighted by a $4 million annual allocation for these services under its waiver programs.

This guide walks you through every step of launching an Adult Day Care Center in South Carolina, from understanding DHEC regulations and licensing to staffing, securing reimbursement, and preparing for inspections. Whether you’re a healthcare professional or an entrepreneur with a passion for serving your community, this is your roadmap to success.

Table of Contents

  • Understand South Carolina’s Adult Day Care Center Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing

  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand South Carolina’s Adult Day Care Center Regulations

Before you can serve a single client, you must have a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape. South Carolina regulates Adult Day Care Centers through the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC), which is responsible for the licensing and regulation of Adult Day Care Facilities under Regulation 60-75, covering safety, staffing, and service provision. This regulation is the foundational document for all compliance activities.

Providers serving Medicaid or federally funded populations must also comply with federal frameworks, including regulations from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) for 1915(c) Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) waivers and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) for protecting client information. The state’s regulatory framework emphasizes promoting independence, reducing institutionalization risks, and ensuring participant safety through comprehensive requirements for health monitoring, activities, and care planning. Licenses are not a one-time event; they typically require renewal every year.

Navigating these dense regulations can be challenging. A misstep in interpreting DHEC’s rules can lead to significant delays or application denial.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Not all Adult Day Care Centers are the same. South Carolina supports multiple program models, allowing you to tailor your services to meet specific community needs. While DHEC provides a single license type, successful providers often create specialized programs. These program type variants include:

  • General Adult Day Care: Provides a broad range of social, recreational, and health-monitoring services for adults who need supervision and assistance during the day.
  • Specialized Alzheimer’s and Dementia Care: Caters specifically to individuals with cognitive impairments. This model requires lower staff-to-client ratios (1:5), specialized staff training, and a secure environment to prevent wandering.
  • Centers for Adults with Physical Disabilities: Focuses on providing accessible facilities, rehabilitative therapies (physical, occupational), and assistance with activities of daily living for clients with mobility challenges.
  • Programs with Behavioral Health Integration: Offers services for adults with co-occurring mental or behavioral health conditions, often integrating counseling and behavioral support into the daily activity schedule.

Program size typically ranges from serving 15 to 50+ participants daily, largely dictated by the physical space available. The regulations mandate a minimum of 60 square feet per participant. Demand is strongest in urban centers like Charleston, Columbia, and Greenville, where waitlists are common. However, rural and underserved regions may offer significant entry opportunities with less competition, especially if you can solve the transportation barrier for clients.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Establishing a solid legal and administrative foundation is a critical early step. In South Carolina, providers typically operate as LLCs, S-Corporations, or non-profits. Your choice of entity will have implications for liability, taxation, and governance. Regardless of the structure, you must complete several key administrative tasks:

  • Register your business with the South Carolina Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS, which is necessary for hiring employees and opening a business bank account.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including general liability, professional liability (errors and omissions), and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a complete licensing application to the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC), including architectural plans, operational policies, and an application fee of approximately $500.

Be prepared for a thorough review process. The licensing timeline in South Carolina generally ranges from 3 to 6 months, depending on the completeness of your application, the time required for facility inspections, and DHEC’s current processing volume. Any missing information or policy gaps will cause delays.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A detailed business plan is your blueprint for success, essential for securing funding and guiding your operational strategy. Startup costs in South Carolina typically range from $75,000 to $250,000 or more, depending on whether you lease or purchase a facility, the extent of renovations needed, and your initial marketing and staffing ramp-up.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by staffing. In this industry, staffing represents the largest line item, often accounting for 50-60% of total costs. Your financial projections must be realistic and account for all expenses, from rent and utilities to insurance and activity supplies.

Your revenue will come from a mix of sources. A typical revenue snapshot for a South Carolina Adult Day Care Center includes:

  • Medicaid Reimbursement: The primary source for many centers, with rates ranging from $60 to $80 per participant per day. The rate is scheduled to increase from $64/day to $80/day on October 1, 2025, representing a significant future revenue boost.
  • Private Pay: Clients who do not qualify for Medicaid pay out-of-pocket. These rates are typically higher than Medicaid, often ranging from $80 to $120 per day.
  • Veterans Affairs (VA) Benefits: The VA may cover adult day health care for eligible veterans.

With strong management and consistent marketing, providers operating at a target occupancy of 70-80% can generally achieve healthy 15% to 25% profit margins. Most centers can expect to reach break-even within 12 to 18 months of opening.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Your physical location is more than just a building; it’s a core component of your service delivery and a major factor in your DHEC licensure. The facility must be safe, accessible, and conducive to your clients’ well-being. Key facility requirements in South Carolina include:

  • A minimum of 60 square feet of usable indoor space per participant, excluding hallways, offices, and storage areas.
  • Full compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), ensuring wheelchair accessibility in entrances, hallways, and restrooms.
  • Adherence to all state and local fire safety codes, verified through an inspection by the fire marshal.
  • Sufficient, accessible restrooms for all participants.
  • Designated areas for group activities, dining, and a quiet space for rest.
  • A secure outdoor area is highly recommended for client recreation.

When selecting a location, consider more than just the building itself. Zoning approval is a prerequisite, so check with the local municipality before signing a lease or purchase agreement. Proximity to hospitals, senior housing communities, and major residential areas can facilitate referrals and make your center more convenient for families. Finally, ensure the location is accessible for your workforce and has adequate parking.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Your staff is the heart of your Adult Day Care Center. DHEC has specific requirements for qualifications, training, and staffing ratios to ensure client safety and quality of care. Required roles typically include:

  • Administrator: Must have a Bachelor’s degree in a health-related field and at least two years of supervisory experience. This person is responsible for overall operations and compliance.
  • Direct Care Staff: Must be at least 18 years old with a high school diploma or equivalent. They are the frontline caregivers responsible for assisting participants with daily activities.
  • Nursing Staff (RN or LPN): Required to meet specific staff-to-client ratios and oversee health-related services like medication administration and health monitoring.

DHEC mandates strict staff-to-client ratios: 1:8 for general supervision, 1:5 for clients with dementia, and 1:20 for nursing oversight. You must schedule staff to meet these ratios at all times. Training requirements are also rigorous and include an initial 40 hours of orientation and job-specific training before a staff member can work independently, followed by 12 hours of ongoing continuing education annually. All employees must pass SLED (South Carolina Law Enforcement Division) and FBI background checks before hire.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive, well-written policies and procedures are the backbone of a compliant operation. They are the first thing a DHEC surveyor will ask to see during an inspection. South Carolina requires written policies covering all aspects of your operation, including:

  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria
  • Participant Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Medication Management and Administration Protocols
  • Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan (including fire, medical emergencies, and elopement)
  • Infection Control and Prevention
  • Staffing Plans, Job Descriptions, and Training Programs
  • Incident Reporting and Investigation
  • Individualized Care Planning and Service Delivery

Beyond operational policies, individual care or service plans are mandatory for every participant. These plans must be person-centered, developed in collaboration with the client and their family, and detail the specific services, goals, and interventions for that individual. These plans are living documents that must be reviewed and updated regularly per South Carolina and federal rules to reflect any changes in the client’s condition or needs.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Once you are licensed, you need to fill your center with clients. In the adult day care industry, marketing is less about consumer advertising and more about building strategic relationships. Your primary referral sources in South Carolina will be:

  • South Carolina Medicaid’s Community Long Term Care (CLTC) case managers, who assess individuals for waiver eligibility and authorize services.
  • Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) that administer Medicaid benefits, such as Absolute Total Care, Magnolia Health, and BlueChoice HealthPlan.
  • Hospital discharge planners and social workers looking for safe, community-based options for patients being discharged.
  • Physicians’ offices, especially neurologists, geriatricians, and primary care providers who treat the target population.
  • Local Area Agencies on Aging and other senior resource centers.
  • Support groups for caregivers, such as those affiliated with the Alzheimer’s Association.

Successful providers focus on demonstrating their value through compliance, responsiveness, and positive client outcomes. Schedule meetings with case managers and discharge planners. Host open houses to showcase your facility and introduce your team. Building a reputation as a reliable, high-quality partner is the most effective marketing strategy.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Receiving your license is the beginning, not the end, of your compliance journey. Oversight is ongoing and includes unannounced inspections from surveying bodies, primarily the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC). These inspections are thorough and focus on ensuring you are adhering to every aspect of Regulation 60-75.

Surveyors often focus on areas where providers most frequently fall short. Common deficiencies found during inspections include:

  • Inadequate staffing ratios, particularly during shift changes or for specialized dementia care.
  • Incomplete or outdated staff training records and background checks.
  • Deficiencies in individual care plans, such as a lack of quarterly reviews or missing participant signatures.
  • Errors in medication administration, documentation, or storage.
  • Incomplete fire safety drill logs or other emergency preparedness documentation.

To avoid citations, you must foster a culture of continuous quality improvement. Conduct regular self-audits, keep your documentation audit-ready at all times, and address any small issues before they become major compliance problems. Being perpetually prepared for a survey is the key to long-term operational stability.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open an Adult Day Care Center in South Carolina?

A: The entire process, from initial business planning to opening your doors, typically takes 12 to 18 months. The DHEC licensing application and review process itself accounts for 3 to 6 months of that timeline, assuming your application and facility are fully prepared.

Q: What licenses are required to operate?

A: You must obtain an Adult Day Care Facility license from the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC). This license is governed by Regulation 60-75 and must be renewed annually.

Q: What reimbursement is available for adult day care services?

A: Reimbursement is primarily available through South Carolina’s 1915(c) Medicaid HCBS waivers, such as the Community Choices and Community Supports waivers. These are often administered by Managed Care Organizations. Current Medicaid rates range from $60-$80 per participant per day. Centers also accept private pay clients and may be able to bill the VA for eligible veterans.

Conclusion

Starting an Adult Day Care Center in South Carolina is a challenging but immensely rewarding venture. The market shows clear signs of strong and growing demand, offering a viable path for entrepreneurs dedicated to providing high-quality community-based care. Success requires careful planning, a deep understanding of DHEC regulations, and a steadfast commitment to operational discipline. Providers who invest in compliance, develop a well-trained and compassionate staff, and build strong referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and a meaningful impact on the lives of South Carolina’s seniors and adults with disabilities.
